stem:
Stimulus: Glucose and galactose are monosaccharides with the same molecular formula, C6H12O6, but their atoms are arranged differently, so the two molecules have different three-dimensional shapes. A transport protein in the plasma membrane of a bacterium moves galactose into the cell efficiently but moves glucose across the membrane very poorly.

Question: Which statement best explains how this transport protein can distinguish between the two sugars?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucose is a polysaccharide, so it is too large to fit through the transport protein that moves galactose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Galactose has hydroxyl groups that glucose lacks, and the transport protein recognizes those extra groups on galactose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galactose contains more carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms than glucose, so the transport protein holds on to it more strongly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two sugars have the same atoms arranged differently, so their shapes differ and only galactose fits the transport protein.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Glucose is a monosaccharide, like galactose, not a polysaccharide.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sugars have the same number of hydroxyl groups; what differs is how the atoms are arranged.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The stimulus states that both sugars have the molecular formula C6H12O6, so their atom counts are the same.
rationales.D: Correct. The same atoms in a different arrangement give each sugar a different three-dimensional shape, and a transport protein can fit one shape much better than the other.

stem:
Stimulus: Yeast cells have a transport protein in the plasma membrane that moves sugar A into the cell efficiently but moves sugar B very poorly. Sugars A and B are monosaccharides with the same molecular formula, C6H12O6, but their atoms are arranged differently. A third monosaccharide, sugar C, also has the formula C6H12O6. Its atoms are arranged so that its molecule has nearly the same three-dimensional shape as sugar A.

Question: Which prediction about the transport of sugar C is best supported by this information?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sugar C will be moved efficiently only after it is broken down into smaller molecules by hydrolysis first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sugar C will be moved into the cells efficiently, because its three-dimensional shape is nearly the same as sugar A's.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sugar C will be moved as poorly as sugar B, because all three sugars have the same molecular formula.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sugar C will be moved poorly, because it has a different molecular formula from the formula of sugar A.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Sugar C is a monosaccharide, a single monomer. Hydrolysis breaks bonds between monomers, and a monosaccharide has no such bond to break.
rationales.B: Correct. The transport protein distinguishes the sugars by shape. A molecule with nearly the same shape as sugar A should fit the protein about as well as sugar A does.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Sugars A and B also share a formula, yet the protein moves sugar A efficiently. The formula is not what the protein distinguishes; shape is.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The stimulus states that sugar C has the same molecular formula, C6H12O6, as sugar A.
